learn: The alphabet is all the letters we use to write. There are 26 letters. They go in order, from A to Z.
We can sing the letters to remember the order. A, B, C, D, E, F, G... Sing slowly and point to each letter as you sing it.
Every letter has a name. The first letter is A. The last letter is Z. M is in the middle.
check: How many letters are in the alphabet?
What is the first letter of the alphabet?
What is the last letter of the alphabet?
lessons.try: Sing the alphabet song and touch each letter on an alphabet chart as you sing.

learn: Each letter can be written two ways. The big one is called uppercase. The small one is called lowercase.
Uppercase B looks like this: B. Lowercase b looks like this: b. They have the same name and the same sound.
We use an uppercase letter at the start of a name, like Sam or Mia. Most other letters in words are lowercase.
check: What do we call a big letter?
What do we call a small letter?
Where do we use an uppercase letter?
At the start of a name
In the middle of every word
lessons.try: Find an uppercase and a lowercase letter in your name. Write them both.

learn: Letters are all around you. Look at signs, cereal boxes, books, and shirts. They all have letters.
A stop sign has the letters S, T, O, P. A box of milk has letters that spell milk.
Your name is made of letters too. The letters in your name are special to you. Learn to find them anywhere.
check: What letters are on a stop sign?
What is your name made of?
lessons.try: Go on a letter hunt in your room. How many letters from your name can you find?

learn: Today we meet the first six letters: A, B, C, D, E and F.
A is for apple. B is for ball. C is for cat. D is for dog. E is for egg. F is for fish.
Look at each letter's shape. A has a point at the top. B has two bumps. C is open like a mouth.
check: Which letter is open like a mouth?
lessons.try: Draw an apple, a ball and a cat. Write the first letter under each picture.

learn: The next letters are G, H, I, J, K and L.
G is for goat. H is for hat. I is for igloo. J is for jam. K is for kite. L is for lion.
L is made of two straight lines. J has a hook at the bottom. I is one tall line.
check: Which letter has a hook at the bottom?
Which letter is made of two straight lines that meet at the bottom?
lessons.try: Make the letter L with two pencils and the letter I with one.

learn: Now we learn M, N, O, P, Q and R.
M is for moon. N is for nest. O is for octopus. P is for pig. Q is for queen. R is for rabbit.
O is a round circle. M has two hills. N has one hill. Q looks like O with a little tail.
check: Which letter is a round circle?
Which letter looks like O with a tail?
lessons.try: Trace the letter O in the air with your finger, then trace Q and add its tail.

learn: The last letters are S, T, U, V, W, X, Y and Z.
S is for sun. T is for top. U is for umbrella. V is for van. W is for web. X is in box. Y is for yo-yo. Z is for zebra.
Z is the last letter of the alphabet. W looks like two V letters side by side.
check: Which letter is the last letter?
Which letter looks like two Vs side by side?
lessons.try: Say a word for each letter from S to Z. Clap once for each word.

learn: Some letters are made only of straight lines. L, T, I, E, F and H are straight-line letters.
When we write, we start at the top. Pull down, then go across.
Hold your pencil with your thumb and pointer finger. Rest it on your middle finger.
check: Where do we start most letters?
Which letter is made only of straight lines?
lessons.try: Write L, T and H three times each. Start at the top every time.

learn: Some letters have curves. C, O, S and G are curvy letters.
To write C, start near the top and curve around to the left, like a backward circle.
S is a snake. Start at the top, curve left, then curve right.
check: Which way do we curve to write C?
lessons.try: Write C, O and S in sand, salt or shaving cream with your finger.

learn: ABC order means putting things in the same order as the alphabet.
A comes before B. B comes before C. If two words start with A and C, the A word comes first.
Libraries and dictionaries use ABC order so we can find things fast.
check: What comes first in ABC order?
Which word comes first: dog or ant?
Why do libraries use ABC order?
lessons.try: Put three picture cards in ABC order: cat, apple, bus.

learn: Your name is the most important word you can write.
A name starts with an uppercase letter. The rest of the letters are lowercase.
Count the letters in your name. Sam has three letters. Isabella has eight.
check: How many letters are in Sam?
The rest of the letters in a name are usually...
lessons.try: Write your name. Count the letters and write the number next to it.

learn: Our classmates have names too. Some names start with the same letter as yours.
Mia and Max both start with M. Ben and Bella both start with B.
We can sort names by their first letter, just like sorting toys by color.
check: Mia and Max both start with...
What can we sort names by?
lessons.try: Write two friends' names. Circle the first letter of each.

learn: Letters make words. Numbers tell how many.
A, B and C are letters. 1, 2 and 3 are numbers.
Some look alike. The letter O and the number 0 are both round. The letter S and the number 5 look a little alike.
check: Which number looks like the letter O?
lessons.try: Look at a page of a book. Point to a letter, then point to a number.

learn: Let's play I Spy with letters. I spy a letter with one tall line and a dot: i.
I spy a letter that starts snake: s. I spy the letter at the start of your name.
Playing games helps your brain remember the letters.
check: Why do we play letter games?
lessons.try: Play I Spy with letters with someone at home. Take turns.

learn: This week you learned all 26 letters, uppercase and lowercase.
You can sing them in order, find them in your world and write many of them.
Practice a little every day. Point to letters when you see them on signs and boxes.
check: How many letters are in the alphabet?
lessons.try: Write as many uppercase letters as you can in order from A. How far did you get?

learn: Letters have names, and they also make sounds. The letter m says /m/, like at the start of moon.
The letter s says /s/, like a snake: sssss. The letter t says /t/, like at the start of top.
When we know letter sounds, we can begin to read words. Sounds are the building blocks of reading.
check: Which letter sounds like a snake?
Why do we learn letter sounds?
lessons.try: Say the sound of m, s and t. Think of a word that starts with each one.

learn: Every word begins with a sound. Say dog slowly: d-o-g. The first sound is /d/.
Say fish slowly. The first sound is /f/. That sound goes with the letter f.
Good listeners stretch words out like a rubber band so they can hear each sound.
check: What is the first sound in dog?
What is the first sound in fish?
How can we hear each sound in a word?
Say it slowly, like stretching a rubber band
lessons.try: Say these words slowly and tell the first sound: ball, cat, pig.

learn: Some letters make sounds that are close. B says /b/ like ball. P says /p/ like pan.
Put your hand in front of your mouth. Say /p/. You feel a puff of air. Say /b/. Your throat buzzes a little.
D and T are close too. D says /d/ like dog. T says /t/ like ten. Listen closely to tell them apart.
check: Which sound makes a puff of air?
lessons.try: Say bat and pat. Which one starts with a puff of air?

learn: The letter a can say /a/, like at the start of apple and ant.
Open your mouth wide and say /a/ /a/ /a/. It sounds like a little baby crying.
Cat, hat and map all have the /a/ sound in the middle.
check: What sound does a make in apple?
Which word has /a/ in the middle?
lessons.try: Say cat, hat and map. Clap when you hear /a/.

lessons.t: The Sounds of B and C
learn: B says /b/, like bear and bus. Your lips pop together.
C often says /k/, like cat, cup and cake.
When you hear /k/ at the start of cat, the letter is c.
check: What sound does c make in cat?
lessons.try: Find three things at home that start with /b/.

lessons.t: The Sounds of D, F and G
learn: D says /d/ like duck. F says /f/ like fan. G says /g/ like goat.
For /f/, put your top teeth on your bottom lip and blow.
For /g/, the sound comes from the back of your throat.
check: Which sound uses teeth on your lip?
lessons.try: Say duck, fan and goat. Tell which letter starts each word.

lessons.t: The Sounds of H, J, K and L
learn: H says /h/, like a little breath: hat, hen. J says /j/ like jet.
K says /k/ like kite. K and c can make the same sound.
L says /l/ like lamp. Your tongue touches the top of your mouth.
check: Which two letters can both say /k/?
lessons.try: Hold your hand near your mouth and say /h/. Can you feel your breath?

lessons.t: The Sounds of N, P and R
learn: N says /n/ like nose. Your tongue touches behind your top teeth and the sound hums.
P says /p/ like pan, with a puff of air. R says /r/ like run, like a growling dog.
Nap, pen and red begin with n, p and r.
check: Which sound growls like a dog?
lessons.try: Growl like a dog: /r/ /r/ /r/. Now say run, red and rug.

lessons.t: The Sounds of V, W, Y and Z
learn: V says /v/ like van. Your lips buzz on your teeth.
W says /w/ like wagon. Y says /y/ like yes. Z says /z/ like a buzzing bee.
These sounds are less common, so we practice them a lot.
check: Which sound is like a buzzing bee?
lessons.try: Buzz like a bee: /z/ /z/ /z/. Say zoo and zip.

lessons.t: The Sounds of Qu and X
learn: Q almost always comes with u. Together, qu says /kw/ like queen and quilt.
X often comes at the end of words. In box and fox, x says /ks/.
These letters are a little tricky, but now you know their secret.
check: What sound does x make in box?
lessons.try: Say queen, quack and quilt. Then say box, fox and six.

learn: Words have ending sounds too. Say cat slowly: c-a-t. The last sound is /t/.
Say bus. The last sound is /s/. Say ham. The last sound is /m/.
Listening for the end of a word helps us spell it all the way.
check: What is the last sound in cat?
What is the last sound in bus?
What is the last sound in ham?
lessons.try: Say pig, sun and cup. Tell the last sound of each.

learn: When we see a picture, we can say its name and listen for the first sound.
A picture of a sun goes with s. A picture of a moon goes with m.
This is how readers and writers connect sounds and letters.
check: A picture of a sun goes with...
A picture of a moon goes with...
A picture of a dog goes with...
lessons.try: Cut pictures from an old magazine. Glue each one next to its first letter.

learn: A sound hunt is a game where you look for things that start with one sound.
On a /t/ hunt you might find a table, a toy and a towel.
Good hunters say each word slowly and check the first sound.
check: On a /m/ hunt you might find...
lessons.try: Go on a /t/ hunt at home and draw the three best things you find.

learn: We can sing a sound song: A says /a/, apple, apple. B says /b/, ball, ball.
Singing helps the sounds stick in our heads.
Clap on each sound as you sing.
check: In the sound song, A says...
Why do we sing the sounds?
lessons.try: Make up your own verse for the first letter of your name.

learn: You can now say a sound for every letter.
You can hear first sounds and last sounds in words.
Knowing sounds is your key to reading.
check: What is the first sound in sun?
What is the last sound in dog?
lessons.try: Read the sounds in your name one by one, then say your name fast.

learn: Five letters are special. They are called vowels: a, e, i, o, u.
Every word needs at least one vowel. The word cat has the vowel a. The word sun has the vowel u.
All the other letters are called consonants. B, c, d, f and g are consonants.
check: What do we call letters that are not vowels?
lessons.try: Clap once for each vowel as you say them: a, e, i, o, u.

learn: Short a says /a/ as in apple. Open your mouth wide and say /a/.
Short e says /e/ as in egg. Short i says /i/ as in itch, or in the middle of pig.
Listen for the vowel in the middle of small words. Cat has /a/. Pet has /e/. Sit has /i/.
check: What sound is in the middle of cat?
Short e says the sound in...
lessons.try: Say map, red and fin. Tell the vowel sound in each.

learn: Short o says /o/ as in octopus. Your mouth makes a round shape.
Short u says /u/ as in up and umbrella. It is a short, quick sound.
Hot has short o. Bug has short u. Now you know all five short vowels!
check: Short u says the sound in...
lessons.try: Say dog, mop, cup and bus. Sort them into short o words and short u words.

learn: Five letters are special. They are called vowels: a, e, i, o and u.
Every word has at least one vowel. The vowel is the heart of the word.
All the other letters are called consonants.
check: How many vowels do we learn?
lessons.try: Write a, e, i, o, u in red. Write b, c and d in blue.

learn: Short e says /e/, like in egg, bed and pen.
Your mouth smiles a little when you say /e/.
Ten, red and net all have short e.
lessons.try: Say bed, pen and ten. Point to e in each word.

learn: Short i says /i/, like in itch, pig and sit.
It is a quick, small sound. Say it fast: /i/ /i/ /i/.
Big, pin and fish all have short i.
check: Which word rhymes with big and has short i?
lessons.try: Wiggle like a worm while you say /i/ words: wig, big, dig.

learn: Short o says /o/, like when the doctor asks you to say ahh: hot, pot, dog.
Make your mouth into a big round O.
Mop, top and box all have short o.
check: When we say /o/, our mouth is...
lessons.try: Say /o/ like at the doctor. Then say hot, mop and box.

learn: Short u says /u/, like in up, cup and bus.
It sounds like a grunt when you lift something heavy: uh!
Sun, mud and bug all have short u.
lessons.try: Pretend to lift a heavy box and say uh. Then say sun, mud and bug.

learn: Many small words have a vowel in the middle: c-a-t, p-i-g, s-u-n.
Stretch the word, then stop on the middle sound.
That middle sound tells you which vowel to write.
check: What is the middle sound in sun?
What is the middle sound in pig?
What is the middle sound in hen?
lessons.try: Say hat, hen, hit, hot and hut. Name the middle vowel in each.

learn: Sorting means putting things that are alike together.
We can sort words by their vowel. Cat and map go together. Pig and sit go together.
Sorting helps us hear the small differences between vowels.
lessons.try: Sort these words into two groups: cat, pig, map, sit, bag, lip.

learn: Change one vowel and you get a new word. Bat becomes bit, then but.
Pan, pen and pin are three words that only change the middle.
This is like a magic trick with letters.
check: Change a in bat to i. What word?
Pan, pen and pin change only the...
Change o in hot to a. What word?
lessons.try: Start with hat. Change the vowel to make hit, hot and hut.

learn: We can sing the short vowel song: a, apple; e, egg; i, itch; o, octopus; u, up.
Make a motion for each one: bite an apple, crack an egg, scratch an itch, wave octopus arms, point up.
Moving your body helps your brain remember.
check: In the song, e is for...
In the song, o is for...
lessons.try: Sing the vowel song with the motions three times.

learn: Look at a picture of a bed. Say it: bed. The middle sound is /e/, so the vowel is e.
A picture of a bug has u. A picture of a cap has a.
Pictures help us practice without reading yet.
lessons.try: Draw a bed, a bug and a cap. Write the vowel under each one.

learn: Now we can find vowels in real words in books.
In the word dog, the vowel is o. In the word sit, the vowel is i.
Every word you read has a vowel hiding inside.
check: What is the vowel in dog?
What is the vowel in sit?
Every word has at least one...
lessons.try: Find five small words in a book and circle the vowel in each.

learn: You know all five short vowels: a, e, i, o and u.
You can hear them in the middle of words and change them to make new words.
Vowels are the heart of every word.
check: How many short vowels are there?
lessons.try: Say one word for each short vowel and tell a grown-up which vowel it has.

learn: Words rhyme when they end with the same sounds. Cat, hat and bat all rhyme. They end in -at.
Rhymes make songs and poems fun to say. "The cat sat on a mat" has lots of rhymes.
To check for a rhyme, say both words and listen to the end. Dog and log rhyme. Dog and cat do not.
check: Where do rhyming words sound the same?
lessons.try: Think of three words that rhyme with pig.

learn: You can make new rhymes by changing the first sound. Start with -ig. Add p for pig. Add w for wig. Add d for dig.
Rhymes can be silly words too. Jig, zig and fig all rhyme with big.
Poets choose rhymes to make their words sing. You can be a poet!
check: Change the p in pig to w. What word do you get?
Who uses rhymes to make words sing?
lessons.try: Make rhymes for -op: start with h, m and t.

learn: Words have parts called syllables. Each part is one beat, like a clap.
Dog has one clap. Ap-ple has two claps. But-ter-fly has three claps.
Put your hand under your chin. Your chin drops once for each syllable you say.
check: How many syllables are in dog?
How many syllables are in butterfly?
lessons.try: Clap the syllables in your name and in elephant.

learn: Words rhyme when their endings sound the same. Cat and hat rhyme.
Only the beginning sound changes: c-at, h-at, b-at.
Poems and songs use rhymes to make them fun to say.
check: Rhyming words sound the same at the...
lessons.try: Say three words that rhyme with cat.

learn: Listen to two words. Do they rhyme? Pig and wig rhyme. Pig and pot do not.
Check the ending. If the endings match, it is a rhyme.
Give a thumbs up for a rhyme and a thumbs down for no rhyme.
lessons.try: Play thumbs up or down with these pairs: bed and red, cup and cat, log and dog.

learn: To make a rhyme, keep the ending and change the first sound.
Start with -an. Add c: can. Add f: fan. Add m: man.
Silly words can rhyme too: zan, lan. That is fine for a game.
check: To make a rhyme, change the...
lessons.try: Make as many rhymes as you can with -op: top, hop, mop...

learn: Nursery rhymes are short poems with lots of rhymes. Jack and Jill went up the hill.
Jill and hill rhyme. Can you hear them?
Hickory, dickory, dock, the mouse ran up the clock. Dock and clock rhyme.
lessons.try: Say Jack and Jill with a grown-up. Clap on the rhyming words.

learn: A syllable is a beat in a word. Cat has one beat. Rab-bit has two beats.
Clap as you say a word to count its syllables.
Long words like but-ter-fly have three beats.
lessons.try: Clap the syllables in your name.

learn: Let's clap more words. Ap-ple: two claps. Ba-na-na: three claps.
Dog: one clap. Ham-bur-ger: three claps.
You can also tap your chin. Your chin drops on each beat.
lessons.try: Put your hand under your chin and say elephant. How many times did your chin drop?

learn: We can join syllables to make a word. Sun plus shine makes sunshine.
Cup plus cake makes cupcake. Rain plus bow makes rainbow.
Joining small parts helps us read longer words.
lessons.try: Join these: pan and cake, foot and ball, star and fish.

learn: We can also take words apart. Snowman is snow and man.
Take away snow and what is left? Man.
Taking words apart helps us spell them.
lessons.try: Break apart these words: football, bedroom, mailbox.

learn: In rhyme time, one person says a word and the next says a rhyme.
Keep going until nobody can think of one more.
Cat, hat, bat, mat, sat, rat, flat! That is seven rhymes.
check: Which word fits rhyme time for bed?
Which word fits rhyme time for cake?
In rhyme time, the next person says a...
lessons.try: Play rhyme time at home with the word bed.

learn: Swap the first sound of a word to make a new one. Swap /m/ in mat for /s/: sat.
Swap /b/ in bug for /r/: rug.
Swaps and rhymes are cousins: the ending stays the same.
check: When we swap the first sound, the ending...
lessons.try: Swap the first sound of hen to make pen, ten and den.

learn: Sort words by how many syllables they have: one, two or three.
Cat goes in one. Tiger goes in two. Elephant goes in three.
Clap each word before you sort it.
lessons.try: Sort these animals by syllables: dog, monkey, kangaroo, fish, zebra.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Rhymes and Beats
learn: You can hear and make rhymes.
You can clap the syllables in words.
These are big steps to becoming a reader.
check: Rhymes sound the same at the...
lessons.try: Say a rhyme for your name, then clap its syllables.

learn: Reading means putting sounds together. This is called blending.
Look at m-a-p. Say /m/, /a/, /p/. Now say them faster and faster: map! You read a word.
Some readers move a finger under each letter as they say its sound, then slide the finger across to blend.
check: Putting sounds together to read a word
lessons.try: Blend these sounds: /s/ /u/ /n/. What word did you make?

learn: Many first words have three letters: a consonant, a vowel and a consonant. Teachers call them CVC words.
Cat, pen, dig, hop and bug are CVC words. Each has a short vowel in the middle.
When you see a CVC word, say each sound and blend. Soon you will read them fast.
check: What is in the middle of a CVC word?
Read h-o-p. What word is it?
lessons.try: Read these CVC words: pen, dig, hop.

learn: Change one sound and you make a new word. Cat becomes hat when you change /c/ to /h/.
Change the vowel and the word changes too. Hat becomes hit. Hit becomes hot.
Change the last sound. Hot becomes hop. Word ladders like this make you a strong reader.
check: Change the c in cat to h. What word do you get?
Change the a in hat to i. What word do you get?
Change the t in hot to p. What word do you get?
lessons.try: Start with pig. Change one sound at a time to make pin, then pan.

learn: Blending means putting sounds together to make a word. /a/ /t/ blends to at.
/i/ /n/ blends to in. /u/ /p/ blends to up.
Say the sounds slowly, then faster and faster until you hear the word.
lessons.try: Blend these: /i/ /t/, /o/ /n/, /a/ /m/.

learn: Now blend three sounds: /c/ /a/ /t/ makes cat.
/d/ /o/ /g/ makes dog. /s/ /u/ /n/ makes sun.
Touch your shoulder, elbow and hand for each sound, then slide down your arm to blend.
lessons.try: Use your arm to blend /m/ /a/ /p/ and /p/ /i/ /g/.

learn: Words that end in -at are a family: cat, bat, hat, mat, rat, sat.
Read the first letter, then add -at.
Once you know one word in a family, you can read them all.
check: Which word is in the -at family?
Knowing one word in a family helps you...
lessons.try: Read cat, bat, hat, mat and sat to a grown-up.

learn: The -in family: pin, win, tin, fin. The -ig family: pig, big, dig, wig.
Both families have short i in the middle.
Read the first sound, then the family ending.
check: Which word is in the -ig family?
lessons.try: Read pin, win, big and dig. Draw a picture for two of them.

learn: The -op family: top, hop, mop, pop. The -ot family: hot, pot, dot, not.
Both have short o in the middle.
Hop on one foot each time you read an -op word.
check: Which word is in the -ot family?
lessons.try: Read and hop: top, hop, mop, pop.

learn: The -ug family: bug, hug, rug, mug. The -un family: sun, run, fun, bun.
Both have short u in the middle.
Give someone a hug when you read the word hug!
check: Which word is in the -un family?
lessons.try: Read bug, hug, run and fun. Use two of them in a sentence.

learn: The -en family: hen, pen, ten, men. The -et family: net, pet, wet, jet.
Both have short e in the middle.
Count to ten on your fingers when you read ten.
check: Which word is in the -et family?
lessons.try: Read hen, pen, net and pet. Which is an animal?

learn: We can build words with letter cards. Put c, u and p together: cup.
Change one card to make a new word: cup to pup.
Building words is like building with blocks.
check: Change c in cup to p. What word?
Change i in sit to a. What word?
lessons.try: Use letter cards or sticky notes to build sit, then change it to sat and set.

learn: Now read two or three words together: a red hat, the big pig, a hot sun.
Point to each word as you read it.
Reading phrases makes reading smooth like talking.
check: In a red hat, which word tells the color?
In the big pig, the animal is a...
When we read, we point to...
lessons.try: Read: a red hat, the big pig, a hot sun. Draw one of them.

learn: A sentence tells a whole idea. The cat sat. The dog ran.
A sentence starts with an uppercase letter and ends with a period.
Read each word, then say the whole sentence like you are talking.
check: In The dog ran, what did the dog do?
lessons.try: Read: The cat sat on a mat. Act it out!

learn: Silly sentences are fun to read: The pig has a wig. The bug is in a mug.
Silly sentences still follow the rules: uppercase start, period at the end.
Laughing while you read helps you love reading.
check: In The pig has a wig, what does the pig have?
Where is the bug in The bug is in a mug?
Silly sentences still end with a...
lessons.try: Read: The cat has a hat. Then write your own silly sentence.

learn: You can blend sounds to read short words.
You know many word families: -at, -in, -ig, -op, -ot, -ug, -un, -en, -et.
You can read short sentences all by yourself.
check: Which word is in the -at family?
Where did the dog sit? (The big dog sat in the sun.)
lessons.try: Read a short sentence to a grown-up: The big dog sat in the sun.

learn: Some words show up in books again and again. We call them sight words.
Good readers know sight words fast, just by looking. The, a, I, see, can, is and we are sight words.
When you know sight words, reading gets smoother and easier.
check: Words we know fast just by looking
Knowing sight words helps reading be...
lessons.try: Find the word the on a page of any book. How many times does it appear?

learn: Some sight words do not follow the usual sound rules. The word the is one. So are said and was.
We cannot always sound these words out, so we practise them until we just know them.
Look, say, spell and say again: s-a-i-d, said. That helps tricky words stick.
check: Which word is tricky to sound out?
How can we learn a tricky word?
Look, say, spell and say again
Is the word the a sight word?
lessons.try: Look at the word said. Say it, spell it aloud, then say it again.

learn: Sight words help us read whole sentences. "I can see a cat." Most of these words are sight words.
A sentence is a group of words that tells a whole idea. It starts with an uppercase letter and ends with a mark, like a period.
Point to each word as you read. Leave a little space between each word in your mind.
check: How many words are in "I can see a cat"?
lessons.try: Read this sentence and point to each word: We like to go.

learn: Some words are so common that we learn to know them at a glance. These are sight words.
I is a word all by itself. It is always an uppercase I. A is a word too: a cat, a dog.
You will see I and a on almost every page you read.
check: Sight words are words we know...
lessons.try: Find I and a on one page of a book. Count how many you see.

learn: The is the most common word in English. The dog. The sun. The tree.
Is tells about something: The dog is big. The sun is hot.
Snap your fingers each time you read the or is.
check: Which is the most common word in English?
In The dog is big, which word tells about the dog?
lessons.try: Read: The cat is fat. The sun is hot. Snap for the and is.

learn: See is about using your eyes: I see a bird. Like tells what you enjoy: I like cake.
See has two e letters in the middle. Like ends with a silent e.
With I, see and like, you can read many sentences.
check: Which word is about using your eyes?
How many e letters are in see?
Which sentence tells what you enjoy?
lessons.try: Finish the sentences out loud: I see a... I like...

learn: To shows where: I go to school. And joins things: a cat and a dog.
Go means to move from here to there.
These three small words help make longer sentences.
check: In a cat and a dog, which word joins them?
Which word means to move from here to there?
lessons.try: Make a sentence with go and to. Make another with and.

lessons.t: The Words we, you, he, she
learn: We means me and other people. You is the person I talk to.
He is for a boy or man. She is for a girl or woman.
These words take the place of names.
check: Which word means me and other people?
Which word is for a girl?
These words take the place of...
lessons.try: Point to yourself and a friend and say we. Point to a friend and say you.

learn: Can tells what someone is able to do: I can run. It names a thing: It is red.
In tells where: The cat is in the box.
Act out each word: show what you can do, point to it, put something in a cup.
check: Which word tells what you are able to do?
In I can run, what can I do?
lessons.try: Read: I can see it in the box.

learn: My shows that something is yours: my hat, my dog.
Look means to use your eyes on purpose: Look at me! Here means this place: Come here.
Look has two o letters, like two eyes looking at you.
check: Which word shows something is yours?
Come ___. means come to this place.
lessons.try: Point to things and say: Here is my... Look at my...

learn: Some sight words do not sound the way they look. These are tricky words.
Said sounds like sed. Was sounds like wuz. Are sounds like ar.
We learn tricky words by heart, by looking and practicing.
lessons.try: Write said, was and are three times each. Say each word as you write.

learn: Sight words are everywhere: on cereal boxes, signs and in books.
Hunting for them helps your eyes remember them faster.
The faster you know them, the smoother your reading becomes.
check: Where can we find sight words?
Knowing sight words fast makes reading...
lessons.try: Hunt for the, and and is in a book. Make a tally mark for each one.

learn: Now put sight words together: I see a cat. We can go. Look at my dog.
You can read whole sentences when you know sight words and can blend.
Read with expression, like you are talking to a friend.
check: In We like to go to the park, where do we go?
Read with expression means read like...
lessons.try: Read: We like to go to the park. Look at the big dog!

learn: You can make your own little book with sight words.
Each page has a sentence and a picture: I like apples. I like dogs. I like the sun.
A pattern like I like makes your book easy to read.
check: A pattern in a book makes it...
Each page of your book has a sentence and a...
Which is a good sentence for an I like book?
lessons.try: Fold paper into a little book. Write I like... on each page and draw.

lessons.t: Show What You Know: Sight Words
learn: You know many sight words now: I, a, the, is, see, like, to, and, go, we, you, can, my, look, said, was, are.
Tricky words need extra practice.
Keep reading every day and they will become easy.
check: Which word names the person I am talking to?
lessons.try: Read your sight word list to a grown-up as fast as you can.

learn: A book has a front cover, a back cover and pages. The cover protects the pages.
The title is the name of the book. It is on the front cover, usually in big letters.
The spine is the side that holds the pages together. On a bookshelf, you often see the spine.
lessons.try: Pick up a book. Point to the front cover, the back cover, the spine and the title.

learn: The author is the person who writes the words of a book.
The illustrator is the person who draws or paints the pictures.
Sometimes one person does both jobs. Beatrix Potter wrote and painted The Tale of Peter Rabbit.
check: Who wrote and painted The Tale of Peter Rabbit?
lessons.try: Look at a book cover. Find the names of the author and the illustrator.

learn: In English we read from left to right. We start at the top of the page and go down.
When we get to the end of a line, we sweep back to the left and start the next line.
We turn pages one at a time, from the front of the book to the back.
check: Which way do we read in English?
Where do we start on a page?
One at a time, front to back
lessons.try: Use your finger to show how your eyes move across a page.

learn: We hold a book with the front cover facing us and the spine on the left.
The words should be right side up. If the pictures are upside down, flip the book.
We turn pages one at a time, gently, from the corner.
check: Where is the spine when we hold a book?
If the pictures are upside down, we...
lessons.try: Show a grown-up how to hold a book and turn three pages gently.

learn: The title is the name of the book. It is on the front cover.
The title tells us what the book might be about. The Very Hungry Caterpillar is about a caterpillar.
We read the title before we start the story.
check: On the spine only, never the cover
lessons.try: Find the title of three books. Read them with help.

learn: A picture walk means looking at the pictures before reading the words.
We guess what will happen. We notice the characters and places.
A picture walk gets our brains ready to read.
check: On a picture walk we look at the...
A picture walk helps our brains get...
On a picture walk we guess...
lessons.try: Take a picture walk through a new book. Tell what you think will happen.

learn: Words tell the story. Pictures show the story.
Sometimes a picture shows something the words do not say, like a hiding mouse.
Good readers look at both.
lessons.try: Find a page where the picture shows something the words do not.

learn: In English, we read words from left to right.
When we reach the end of a line, we sweep back to the left for the next line.
We read the top of the page before the bottom.
check: At the end of a line we...
We read the ___ of the page first.
lessons.try: Run your finger under the words as a grown-up reads. Sweep back at the end of each line.

learn: Letters make words. Spaces between words show where one word ends.
Count the words in a sentence by counting the groups of letters.
The cat sat. That is three words.
check: How many words in The cat sat.?
How many words in I like my red hat.?
lessons.try: Count the words in: I like my red hat.

learn: A library is a place full of books we can borrow for free.
We take care of library books and bring them back on time.
The librarian helps us find good books.
lessons.try: Visit the school library and find one book about animals.

learn: A good book for you is one you like and can understand.
Look at the cover, the title and a few pages.
You can choose books about things you love, like dinosaurs or princesses.
check: A good book for you is one you...
To choose a book, look at the...
Can you pick books about things you love?
lessons.try: Pick two books and tell why you chose each one.

learn: Reading with a partner is fun. One reads, one listens, then switch.
We sit side by side and share the book so both can see.
Good listeners look at the book and do not interrupt.
check: We sit ___ to share a book.
lessons.try: Read a book with a partner. Take turns reading the pages.

learn: Readers read every day, even just for a few minutes.
You can read to a pet, a stuffed animal or a little brother or sister.
The more you read, the better you get.
lessons.try: Make a reading chart. Color a box each day you read this week.

learn: Books last a long time when we care for them.
Keep books away from food, water and pets. Use a bookmark, not a folded corner.
Put books back on the shelf when you finish.
check: To save your place, use a...
When you finish, put the book...
lessons.try: Make a bookmark out of paper and decorate it.

learn: You know how to hold a book, find the title, read left to right and care for books.
You know authors write and illustrators draw.
You are a real reader!
lessons.try: Show a grown-up the cover, title, author and first page of your favorite book.

learn: Characters are the people or animals in a story. In The Three Little Pigs, the pigs and the wolf are characters.
The main character is the one the story is mostly about.
Characters have feelings. They can be happy, scared, brave or silly. We learn about them from what they say and do.
check: The people or animals in a story
Who are the characters in The Three Little Pigs?
How do we learn about characters?
From what they say and do
lessons.try: Think of a story you love. Who is the main character?

learn: The setting is where and when a story happens.
A setting could be a farm, a city, a forest, a castle or under the sea. It could be at night or in winter.
Pictures often show the setting. Look at the trees, the houses and the sky.
check: Where and when the story happens
What often shows us the setting?
lessons.try: Draw the setting of your favourite story.

learn: A story has events. Events are the things that happen.
Something happens first, in the beginning. Then more happens in the middle. The story finishes at the end.
When we retell a story, we say the events in order: first, next, then, last.
check: The things that happen in a story
Which words help us retell in order?
lessons.try: Retell Goldilocks and the Three Bears using first, next, then and last.

learn: The people or animals in a story are the characters.
In The Three Little Pigs, the characters are three pigs and a wolf.
The main character is the one the story is mostly about.
check: The people or animals in a story are the...
Who are the characters in The Three Little Pigs?
The main character is the one the story is...
lessons.try: Name the characters in your favorite story. Who is the main character?

learn: Characters have feelings, just like us. They can be happy, sad, scared or mad.
We can tell how they feel from their faces in the pictures and from the words.
The pigs feel scared when the wolf huffs and puffs.
check: How do the pigs feel when the wolf comes?
We can tell how characters feel from their...
lessons.try: Make a happy face, a sad face and a scared face. When might a character feel each one?

learn: The setting is where and when a story happens.
A story can happen in a forest, a city, a castle or under the sea.
It can happen long ago, today or in the future.
check: The setting is where and ___ a story happens.
lessons.try: Draw the setting of a story you know.

learn: Most stories have a problem. The problem is what goes wrong.
In Goldilocks and the Three Bears, the bears come home and find someone ate their porridge.
The story is about how the problem gets fixed.
check: In Goldilocks, someone ate the bears'...
Stories are often about how the problem gets...
lessons.try: Tell the problem in a story you know.

learn: The solution is how the problem is fixed.
The third little pig built a brick house. The wolf could not blow it down. That is the solution.
Solutions can be clever, brave or kind.
check: The solution is how the problem is...
How did the third pig solve the problem?
lessons.try: Think of another solution the pigs could have tried.

learn: To retell a story, tell what happened in order.
Use the words first, next, then and last.
First the pigs left home. Next they built houses. Then the wolf came. Last the brick house kept them safe.
check: To retell, we tell what happened in...
lessons.try: Retell a story to a grown-up using first, next, then and last.

learn: Sequencing means putting events in order.
Picture cards can help. Look at each card and decide what happened first.
If the order is wrong, the story will not make sense.
check: If the order is wrong, the story will...
Which comes first: planting a seed or eating the apple?
lessons.try: Draw three pictures from a story and put them in order.

learn: Fairy tales are old stories told for many years. They often start with Once upon a time.
Fairy tales may have magic, talking animals, kings, queens and giants.
They often end with happily ever after.
lessons.try: Listen to a fairy tale. Find the magic or the talking animal.

learn: We can compare stories. How are they the same? How are they different?
The Three Little Pigs and The Three Billy Goats Gruff both have three animals and a mean character.
But one has a wolf and houses, and the other has a troll and a bridge.
lessons.try: Tell one way two stories are the same and one way they are different.

learn: Good readers ask questions: Who? What? Where? Why?
Why did Goldilocks go into the house? What will the bears do?
Asking questions keeps us thinking while we read.
check: Good readers ask questions to keep...
lessons.try: Ask two questions about a story a grown-up reads to you.

learn: A prediction is a smart guess about what will happen next.
We use clues from the pictures and the words.
After we read, we check: Was my prediction right?
check: A prediction is a smart guess about...
After reading, we check if the prediction was...
lessons.try: Stop in the middle of a story. Predict what will happen, then read on to check.

learn: Stories have characters, a setting, a problem and a solution.
We can retell stories in order and make predictions.
Stories teach us and make us laugh.
check: Where and when a story happens is the...
How the problem is fixed is the...
A smart guess about what happens next is a...
lessons.try: Tell a grown-up the characters, setting, problem and solution of a story you love.

learn: Some books tell made-up stories. We call them fiction. A talking bear is fiction.
Other books teach true facts. We call them nonfiction. A book about real bears and what they eat is nonfiction.
Nonfiction books often have real photos instead of drawings.
check: A book that teaches true facts
What do nonfiction books often have?
lessons.try: Find one fiction book and one nonfiction book. How can you tell?

learn: The topic is what the whole book is about. A book called Sharks has sharks as its topic.
Every page in a nonfiction book tells something about the topic.
Before reading, look at the cover and the pictures. Guess the topic.
check: What the whole book is about
What is the topic of a book called Sharks?
How can we guess the topic?
Look at the cover and the pictures
lessons.try: Look at a nonfiction book cover and say its topic.

learn: Good readers ask questions before, during and after they read.
Before: What do I think I will learn? During: What does this word mean? After: What was the most interesting fact?
Questions start with words like who, what, where, when, why and how.
check: When do good readers ask questions?
What was the most interesting fact?
lessons.try: Think of a question you would like a book about the moon to answer.

learn: A fact is something that is true. A dog has four legs. The sun is hot.
Nonfiction books are full of facts.
We can check facts in other books or by looking closely.
check: A fact is something that is...
Dogs can fly to the moon.
lessons.try: Tell two facts about an animal you know.

learn: Many nonfiction books have real photographs instead of drawings.
Photos show what things really look like.
A photo of a frog shows its real color and skin.
check: A photo of a frog shows its real...
lessons.try: Find a book with real photos. Tell one thing you learned from a photo.

learn: A table of contents is a list at the front of a book. It tells what is inside.
It shows the name of each part and the page number.
If you want to read about lions, find lions in the list and go to that page.
check: The table of contents is at the...
It shows each part's name and...
The table of contents tells what is...
lessons.try: Use a table of contents to find one part of a nonfiction book.

learn: A label is a word that names part of a picture.
A picture of a bird may have labels for wing, beak, feathers and tail.
Labels teach us the names of things.
check: A label names part of a...
Which label could go on a bird picture?
lessons.try: Draw a picture of yourself and label your head, arms, hands and feet.

learn: A caption is a sentence under a photo that tells about it.
A photo of a whale might have the caption: A blue whale is the biggest animal.
Always read the caption. It often has a fact.
check: A caption is a sentence ___ a photo.
lessons.try: Find a caption in a book or magazine. Read it with help.

learn: Animal books tell where animals live, what they eat and how they grow.
A bear lives in the forest. It eats berries and fish. Baby bears are called cubs.
Animal books help us care about animals.
lessons.try: Choose an animal. Find out where it lives and what it eats.

learn: Nonfiction books teach about weather, plants, space, machines and people.
You can learn how a seed grows or how a truck works.
There is a nonfiction book about almost everything.
check: Is there a nonfiction book about almost everything?
Where can we find nonfiction books?
lessons.try: Pick a topic you wonder about. Find a book about it in the library.

learn: Fiction is a made-up story. Nonfiction gives true facts.
A talking pig in a hat is fiction. A book about how real pigs live is nonfiction.
Ask: Could this really happen? Is it teaching me facts?
check: A talking pig in a hat is...
A book about how real pigs live is...
lessons.try: Sort four books into fiction and nonfiction.

learn: Nonfiction books have special words, like hibernate, which means to sleep through winter.
Pictures and labels help us learn new words.
Ask a grown-up when you find a word you do not know.
check: What can help us learn new words?
When you find a word you do not know, you can...
lessons.try: Find one new word in a nonfiction book. Draw a picture of what it means.

learn: When we learn a fact, we can share it with others.
Say: Did you know that a giraffe has a long neck to reach leaves?
Sharing facts helps everyone learn.
check: Why does a giraffe have a long neck?
A good way to share a fact begins with...
lessons.try: Share three facts you learned this week with your family.

learn: You can make your own nonfiction book.
Pick a topic, write a fact on each page and draw a picture with labels.
Add a title on the cover and your name as the author.
check: Each page of a fact book has a...
Your name on the cover shows you are the...
Pictures in your fact book can have...
lessons.try: Make a three-page fact book about a topic you love.

learn: Nonfiction books give facts, real photos, labels and captions.
A table of contents helps you find things fast.
You can tell fiction from nonfiction.
check: A sentence under a photo is a...
The table of contents helps you...
lessons.try: Show a grown-up a label, a caption and the table of contents in a nonfiction book.

learn: Writers share their ideas with pictures and words.
First, think of your idea. Then draw it. Then add words that tell about your picture.
You can label your drawing. Write sun next to the sun and dog next to the dog.
check: What do writers use to share ideas?
Think of an idea and draw it
A word next to a picture that names it
lessons.try: Draw your favourite animal and label it.

learn: Say your sentence out loud first. Count the words on your fingers.
Write one word at a time. Leave a finger space between words.
A sentence starts with an uppercase letter and ends with a period, a question mark or an exclamation mark.
check: What do we leave between words?
With a period, question mark or exclamation mark
What should we do before writing a sentence?
lessons.try: Write the sentence: I like my cat.

learn: Writers share their work with others. They read it aloud, slowly and clearly.
Listeners can say one thing they liked and ask one question.
Writers can add more after sharing. Maybe add a word, a colour or one more sentence.
check: What can a writer do after sharing?
Add more to make it better
lessons.try: Read your writing to someone and ask them what they liked.

learn: Writers use pencils, crayons and paper. Some use computers too.
Keep your paper flat and hold it with your other hand.
Sit up tall with your feet on the floor.
lessons.try: Show a grown-up how you sit and hold your paper when you write.

learn: Writers start by drawing a picture and adding labels.
Draw your house. Label the door, window and roof.
Say each word slowly and write the sounds you hear.
check: To write a label, say the word...
Which is a label for a house?
lessons.try: Draw your bedroom and label three things.

learn: When we write, we leave a space between words.
Use a finger space: put your finger after a word, then start the next one.
Spaces make writing easy to read.
lessons.try: Write I like dogs. using a finger space between each word.

learn: To spell a word, stretch it like a rubber band: s-u-n.
Write a letter for each sound you hear.
It is okay if the spelling is not perfect. Write the sounds you hear.
check: To spell, we stretch the word like a...
We write a letter for each...
Is it okay if your spelling is not perfect yet?
lessons.try: Stretch and write: map, bus, fin.

learn: A sentence begins with a capital letter. A sentence ends with a period.
The word I is always a capital letter.
Check your writing: Did I start with a capital? Did I end with a period?
lessons.try: Write two sentences and check each one for a capital and a period.

learn: Writers write about what they know. You know a lot about yourself!
Write: My name is... I am ... years old. I like...
Add a drawing of yourself.
check: Which is a sentence about me?
A good writing piece can include a...
lessons.try: Write three sentences about you and draw a picture.

learn: A story has a beginning, a middle and an end.
First tell who and where. Next tell what happened. Last tell how it ended.
Draw a picture for each part.
check: A story has a beginning, a middle and an...
lessons.try: Fold paper into three. Draw and write a beginning, middle and end.

learn: We can write to teach someone a fact.
Write: Cats have whiskers. Cats drink milk. Cats like to nap.
Use a topic word, like cats, at the start of each sentence.
check: Which is a fact sentence about cats?
A topic word tells what the writing is...
lessons.try: Write three facts about an animal.

learn: An opinion is what you think or like. I think pizza is the best food.
Give a reason with because: I like pizza because it is cheesy.
Other people can have different opinions, and that is okay.
lessons.try: Write: My favorite animal is... because...

learn: A thank-you note tells someone you are grateful.
Start with Dear and their name. Say thank you and why. End with Love or From and your name.
Thank-you notes make people feel happy.
check: A thank-you note says thank you and...
At the end of the note, write your...
lessons.try: Write a thank-you note to someone at school or home.

learn: Writers read their writing again to make it better.
Check for capitals, periods, finger spaces and sounds.
Fixing is a normal part of writing. Every writer does it.
check: Writers read their writing again to make it...
Does every writer fix their writing?
lessons.try: Read one of your sentences out loud. Fix one thing to make it better.

learn: You can draw, label and write sentences.
You can write stories, facts, opinions and notes.
You are a writer!
check: An opinion uses a reason with...
lessons.try: Write and draw about your favorite day this year. Share it with your class.
